stem: A 29-year-old man had a painless penile ulcer 6 weeks ago that healed without treatment. He now has a diffuse maculopapular rash including the palms and soles, low-grade fever and malaise. Serum RPR is positive at 1:64 and a treponemal test is positive. He has no drug allergies and receives a single intramuscular injection of the drug of choice.
oneliner: 29M + painless penile ulcer that healed + rash incl. palms and soles + fever + RPR 1:64, treponemal test positive + one IM injection → drug works how?
ask: The drug of choice acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Inhibiting bacterial protein translation
options.B: Inhibiting peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall
options.D: Forming pores in the cell membrane

whyNot.A: **Aminoglycoside / tetracycline / macrolide** mechanism; not first line for syphilis
whyNot.C: **Fluoroquinolone** mechanism; not used for syphilis
whyNot.D: **Polymyxin or daptomycin** mechanism
whyNot.E: **Sulfonamide** mechanism; spirochetes are not treated this way

why: **Healed chancre + palm and sole rash + positive serology** = secondary syphilis. **Benzathine penicillin G** binds **penicillin-binding proteins**, blocks **transpeptidase cross-linking**, and the cell wall fails.

drug.name: Penicillin G (benzathine)
drug.how: Binds penicillin-binding proteins; blocks transpeptidation of peptidoglycan
drug.use: Syphilis, group A strep, Neisseria meningitidis, Actinomyces
drug.watch: Hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis, rash), hemolytic anemia, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction in syphilis

stem: A 32-year-old man with a bicuspid aortic valve has had 3 weeks of fever and fatigue. He has a new diastolic murmur and splinter hemorrhages. Blood cultures grow viridans streptococci that are highly susceptible to penicillin. Treatment is penicillin plus a second drug chosen because it acts synergistically and allows a shorter course.
oneliner: 32M + bicuspid aortic valve + 3 wk fever, new murmur, splinter hemorrhages + viridans strep, penicillin-susceptible + synergistic second drug → works how?
ask: The second drug acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding the 30S ribosomal subunit and causing mRNA misreading

whyNot.B: **Rifampin**: used with other drugs for staphylococcal prosthetic valve, not synergistic with penicillin here
whyNot.C: **Fluoroquinolones**: no synergy with cell wall drugs for viridans strep
whyNot.D: **Trimethoprim**: bacteriostatic folate antagonist, not a synergy partner
whyNot.E: **Macrolide / clindamycin**: bacteriostatic, no synergy with penicillin

why: **Viridans strep endocarditis** is treated with **penicillin plus gentamicin**. Penicillin **damages the wall so the aminoglycoside can enter**; gentamicin then binds **30S**, causing misreading, and the combination is **bactericidal**.

drug.name: Gentamicin
drug.how: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit, causing mRNA misreading; needs oxygen-dependent uptake and wall damage to enter
drug.use: Gram-negative sepsis, synergy with beta-lactams for endocarditis, pyelonephritis
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade, teratogenic (fetal ototoxicity)

stem: A 58-year-old man with urosepsis is receiving gentamicin every 8 hours. His renal function is currently normal. A level drawn after the fourth dose shows a peak of 8.8 mcg/mL (goal 5 to 10) and a trough of 2.5 mcg/mL (goal below 2). He is improving clinically, and the team wants to lower the risk of kidney and ear damage while keeping the effect.
oneliner: 58M + urosepsis on gentamicin q8h + peak 8.8 (goal 5-10) + trough 2.5 (goal <2) + improving → how to adjust?
ask: Which of the following is the most appropriate adjustment?

options.A: Keep the same dose and shorten the interval
options.B: Lower the dose and give it every 6 hours
options.C: Keep the same dose and lengthen the interval
options.D: Raise the dose and keep the interval
options.E: Lower the dose and keep the interval

whyNot.A: Less time to clear drug, so the **trough rises further**
whyNot.B: More frequent dosing keeps the **trough high**
whyNot.D: Raises **both peak and trough**; trough stays too high
whyNot.E: **Peak drops below goal**; killing is concentration dependent

why: **Peak at goal but trough too high** = the drug is accumulating. Aminoglycosides kill in a **concentration-dependent** way, so keep the **peak** and **lengthen the interval** so the trough falls, which **lowers nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity**.

drug.name: Gentamicin
drug.how: Binds 30S ribosomal subunit; concentration-dependent killing with a post-antibiotic effect
drug.use: Serious gram-negative infections
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity linked to high troughs; adjust the interval to renal function

stem: A 52-year-old man who smokes has had 4 days of fever, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. He is stable, with a respiratory rate of 20/min and oxygen saturation of 95% on room air. A chest radiograph shows right middle lobe consolidation. He is treated as an outpatient with azithromycin.
oneliner: 52M + smoker + 4 d fever, cough, pleuritic pain + stable + RML consolidation + azithromycin → works how?
ask: The antibiotic acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding the 30S subunit and blocking aminoacyl-tRNA attachment
options.B: Inhibiting DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
options.C: Inhibiting transpeptidation of the cell wall
options.E: Binding the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocking translocation

whyNot.A: **Tetracycline** mechanism
whyNot.B: **Levofloxacin** mechanism
whyNot.C: **Cefdinir / beta-lactam** mechanism
whyNot.D: **TMP-SMX** mechanism

why: **Fever + productive cough + lobar consolidation** = community-acquired pneumonia. **Azithromycin** binds the **23S rRNA of the 50S subunit** and **blocks translocation**.

drug.name: Azithromycin
drug.how: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation
drug.use: Community-acquired pneumonia, atypicals, Chlamydia, MAC prophylaxis, pertussis
drug.watch: QT prolongation, GI upset, cholestatic hepatitis; less CYP3A4 inhibition than erythromycin

stem: A 17-year-old girl with acne was started on tetracycline 3 weeks ago. There has been no improvement. She takes the tablet every morning with a large glass of milk. She takes no other medication, her adherence is good, and the tablets are in date.
oneliner: 17F + acne on tetracycline 3 wk + no improvement + takes each tablet with a glass of milk + good adherence → why no effect?
ask: Which of the following best explains the lack of response?

options.A: Induction of CYP450 enzymes by milk
options.B: Chelation by calcium in milk, reducing absorption
options.E: Delayed gastric emptying that destroys the drug

whyNot.A: Milk **does not induce** hepatic enzymes
whyNot.C: Milk fat is not the **interacting component**
whyNot.D: Would change the free fraction, **not stop absorption**
whyNot.E: Tetracycline is **not destroyed** in the stomach

answer: Chelation by divalent cations in milk (tetracycline absorption falls)
why: **Tetracycline with milk** forms **insoluble chelates with calcium** and other polyvalent cations (Mg, Fe, Al antacids), so **less is absorbed**. Take it **apart from dairy, antacids and iron**.

drug.name: Tetracycline
drug.how: Binds 30S subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment; chelates divalent cations
drug.use: Acne, Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Mycoplasma, Lyme (doxycycline), H. pylori regimens
drug.watch: Chelation with milk, antacids and iron; photosensitivity; teeth and bone staining; esophagitis

stem: A 28-year-old man has 4 days of fever, severe headache and myalgias after a hiking and camping trip in North Carolina. A rash began on the wrists and ankles and has spread to the palms and soles. Serum sodium is 129 mEq/L and platelets are 90,000/mm3. Empiric therapy is started before laboratory confirmation with a drug that interferes with one step of bacterial protein synthesis.
oneliner: 28M + camping in North Carolina + fever, headache + rash from wrists and ankles to palms and soles + Na 129, platelets 90,000 → which step is blocked?
ask: The drug of choice blocks which step of protein synthesis?

options.A: Peptide bond formation by peptidyl transferase
options.B: Translocation of the ribosome along mRNA
options.E: Attachment of aminoacyl-tRNA to the ribosomal A site

whyNot.A: **Chloramphenicol** blocks this on 50S
whyNot.B: **Macrolides / clindamycin** block this on 50S
whyNot.C: **Linezolid** blocks this by binding the 50S subunit
whyNot.D: **Aminoglycosides** cause misreading; they do not treat intracellular Rickettsia well

answer: Blocked aminoacyl-tRNA binding at the A site (doxycycline)
why: **Tick exposure + rash starting at wrists and ankles and reaching palms and soles + low sodium and platelets** = Rocky Mountain spotted fever. **Doxycycline** blocks **aminoacyl-tRNA** from entering the **30S A site**. Give it **before confirmation**.

drug.name: Doxycycline
drug.how: Binds 30S subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA attachment at the A site
drug.use: Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, chlamydia, Mycoplasma, acne
drug.watch: Photosensitivity, esophagitis, teeth and bone staining, chelation by cations; avoid in pregnancy

stem: A 45-year-old woman has fever, flank pain and costovertebral tenderness. Urine culture grows E. coli. Her fever persists after 3 days of oral ciprofloxacin, and the isolate is found to be resistant. Sequencing shows a point mutation in the gene for the enzyme that the drug normally inhibits.
oneliner: 45F + pyelonephritis + persistent fever on ciprofloxacin + resistant E. coli + point mutation in the drug's target gene → which enzyme?
ask: The mutation most likely affects which of the following bacterial enzymes?

options.A: DNA-dependent RNA polymerase

whyNot.A: **Rifampin** target; mutation here causes rifampin resistance
whyNot.B: **Sulfonamide** target; folate pathway
whyNot.C: **Chloramphenicol** target on the 50S ribosome; protein synthesis, not a DNA enzyme
whyNot.E: **Beta-lactam** target; cell wall synthesis

answer: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II); mutation causes quinolone resistance
why: **Ciprofloxacin resistance from a point mutation in its target gene**: fluoroquinolones inhibit **DNA gyrase (topo II) and topoisomerase IV**, so gyrase mutations lower drug binding.

drug.name: Ciprofloxacin
drug.how: Inhibits DNA gyrase (topo II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication
drug.use: UTI, pyelonephritis, gram-negative rods, Pseudomonas, anthrax
drug.watch: Tendon rupture, QT prolongation, cartilage damage in children, C. difficile, absorption blocked by divalent cations

stem: A 40-year-old man has had 2 months of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Chest film shows an upper-lobe cavity, and sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli. He is started on a four-drug regimen. Two weeks later he notices that his urine, sweat and tears are orange-red.
oneliner: 40M + upper-lobe cavity + AFB on sputum + four-drug regimen + orange-red urine and tears → the responsible drug works how?
ask: The drug that colors his body fluids acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Inhibiting arabinosyl transferase in the cell wall
options.E: Inhibiting mycolic acid synthesis via KatG activation

whyNot.A: **Ethambutol**: causes optic neuritis, not orange secretions
whyNot.B: **Fluoroquinolones**: second-line for TB; do not color fluids
whyNot.C: **Streptomycin / aminoglycosides**: injectable; ototoxic and nephrotoxic
whyNot.E: **Isoniazid**: neuropathy and hepatitis, **not orange body fluids**

why: **Orange-red urine, sweat and tears on a TB regimen** = **rifampin**. It binds the **beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase**, blocking transcription initiation.

drug.name: Rifampin
drug.how: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (beta subunit)
drug.use: TB, leprosy, Neisseria meningitidis prophylaxis, Staph with other drugs
drug.watch: Orange body fluids, hepatitis, strong CYP450 inducer (lowers OCP, warfarin levels)

stem: A 36-year-old man with HIV infection and a CD4 count of 40/µL has had 2 weeks of worsening headache, fever and mild neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 32 cm H2O, a lymphocytic pleocytosis and encapsulated yeast on India ink stain. He is admitted for intravenous induction therapy with a drug that is given with careful monitoring of renal function and potassium.
oneliner: 36M + HIV, CD4 40 + 2 wk headache, fever + high opening pressure + India ink yeast + IV induction drug with renal and K monitoring → drug works how?
ask: The induction drug works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding ergosterol and forming pores in the fungal membrane

whyNot.B: **Fluconazole**: used later for consolidation and maintenance, not for IV induction here
whyNot.C: **Echinocandins**: have **no activity** against this yeast
whyNot.D: **Terbinafine**: dermatophytes and nails, not CNS infection
whyNot.E: **Griseofulvin**: oral drug for tinea; not for meningitis

answer: Binds ergosterol and forms membrane pores (amphotericin B)
why: **HIV with cryptococcal meningitis** needs IV induction with **amphotericin B**, which **binds ergosterol and forms pores** that leak ions, hence the electrolyte and renal monitoring.

drug.name: Amphotericin B
drug.how: Binds ergosterol, forms membrane pores, ions leak out
drug.use: Cryptococcal meningitis (with flucytosine), mucormycosis, severe invasive fungal infections
drug.watch: Infusion fever and chills, nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, anemia

stem: A 58-year-old woman in the ICU has had fever for 5 days after abdominal surgery. Blood cultures grow Candida glabrata resistant to fluconazole. Her serum creatinine is 3.1 mg/dL and rising. An intravenous antifungal that needs no renal adjustment and has few toxicities is chosen.
oneliner: 58F + post-op ICU fever + blood cultures fluconazole-resistant Candida + creatinine 3.1 + IV drug with few toxicities → drug works how?
ask: The drug selected works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding ergosterol in the cell membrane
options.D: Inhibiting fungal DNA and RNA synthesis
options.E: Inhibiting β-(1,3)-glucan synthesis in the cell wall

whyNot.A: **Amphotericin B**: nephrotoxic, a poor choice with creatinine 3.1
whyNot.B: **Azoles**: this isolate is **azole-resistant**
whyNot.C: **Terbinafine**: not used for systemic candidemia
whyNot.D: **Flucytosine**: used only in combination because of rapid resistance

why: **Candidemia that is azole-resistant with kidney injury** points to an **echinocandin** (caspofungin, micafungin). It **blocks β-(1,3)-glucan synthase**, so the cell wall is weakened.

drug.name: Caspofungin
drug.how: Inhibits β-(1,3)-glucan synthase, weakening fungal cell wall
drug.use: Invasive candidiasis (including azole-resistant), invasive aspergillosis (salvage)
drug.watch: IV only, flushing from histamine release, elevated liver enzymes; no activity against Cryptococcus

stem: A 62-year-old man with poorly controlled HIV has painful swallowing, and endoscopy shows white plaques in the esophagus. He is given a single daily tablet and improves in 3 days. Two weeks later his INR on warfarin rises from 2.4 to 5.8, and he has an episode of hypoglycemia on glipizide.
oneliner: 62M + HIV + painful swallowing, esophageal white plaques + daily tablet + INR rises on warfarin, hypoglycemia on glipizide → how does the tablet work?
ask: The drug that was started works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding ergosterol and forming pores

whyNot.A: **Amphotericin B**: given IV, not as a daily tablet
whyNot.B: **Echinocandins**: IV only
whyNot.D: **Terbinafine**: for dermatophytes and nails, not esophageal candidiasis
whyNot.E: **Flucytosine**: not used alone and not taken for this infection

why: **Esophageal candidiasis treated with an oral azole** (fluconazole). It **blocks lanosterol 14α-demethylase**, lowering ergosterol. It also **inhibits CYP2C9**, raising warfarin and glipizide effects.

drug.name: Fluconazole
drug.how: Inhibits fungal CYP51 (lanosterol 14α-demethylase), blocking ergosterol synthesis
drug.use: Candidiasis (oral, esophageal, vaginal), cryptococcal consolidation, coccidioidomycosis
drug.watch: CYP450 inhibition (warfarin, sulfonylureas, phenytoin), hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation, teratogenic

stem: A 45-year-old man had a kidney transplant 6 months ago and takes tacrolimus. For one day he has had tingling and burning at the border of the lip, and today a skin eruption appeared at that site (see image). An oral antiviral is started.
oneliner: 45M + kidney transplant on tacrolimus + 1 day of lip tingling, burning, now skin eruption (image) + oral antiviral → which viral enzyme activates the drug?
ask: Which viral enzyme is needed to activate the drug that was started?

options.A: DNA polymerase

whyNot.A: **DNA polymerase**: the target of the active triphosphate, not the activating enzyme
whyNot.B: **Neuraminidase**: influenza; its inhibitors do not need viral activation
whyNot.C: **Reverse transcriptase**: HIV and HBV; this virus does not use it
whyNot.D: **Protease**: its inhibitors act directly on the enzyme, no phosphorylation needed

answer: Viral thymidine kinase (acyclovir needs it for the first phosphorylation)
why: **Grouped vesicles on the lip with a tingling prodrome in an immunosuppressed host** = herpes simplex. **Acyclovir is first phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase**, so it acts mainly in infected cells.

drug.name: Acyclovir
drug.how: Phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, then terminates viral DNA chain
drug.use: HSV, VZV, HSV encephalitis, herpes zoster
drug.watch: Crystalline nephropathy (hydrate), neurotoxicity; resistance from thymidine kinase mutations

image.prompt: Close-up photograph of a cluster of small grouped fluid-filled vesicles on a red base at the vermilion border of the upper lip in a middle-aged man.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has had 2 days of burning pain along the left lower ribs. Yesterday clustered vesicles on an erythematous base appeared in a band that stops at the midline. She is started on valacyclovir.
oneliner: 72F + burning pain, then band-like vesicles on the left chest stopping at midline + valacyclovir started → how does it work?
ask: The active form of this drug acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Blocking viral neuraminidase
options.D: Terminating chain elongation by viral DNA polymerase

whyNot.A: **Neuraminidase inhibitors**: influenza only
whyNot.B: **Protease inhibitors**: HIV and HCV; not zoster
whyNot.C: **RT inhibitors**: retroviruses; this virus is a DNA virus replicating with its own polymerase
whyNot.E: **Ribavirin**: RSV and hepatitis C, not zoster

answer: Viral DNA polymerase inhibition and DNA chain termination (acyclovir-type drug)
why: **Unilateral dermatomal vesicles** = herpes zoster (VZV). **Valacyclovir** is converted to **acyclovir**, whose triphosphate **inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates the DNA chain**.

drug.name: Valacyclovir (acyclovir prodrug)
drug.how: Activated by viral thymidine kinase; triphosphate inhibits viral DNA polymerase and ends DNA chain
drug.use: Herpes zoster, HSV, genital herpes suppression
drug.watch: Nephrotoxicity (hydrate), neurotoxicity in renal failure; resistance from TK mutations

stem: An 81-year-old woman in a nursing home has had 2 days of fever, cough and myalgias. Five other residents on her floor are similarly ill, and a rapid test of her nasal swab is positive for influenza. All affected residents are given an oral antiviral.
oneliner: 81F + nursing home flu outbreak + fever, cough, myalgia + oral antiviral started → which step in the viral life cycle is blocked?
ask: The antiviral most likely blocks which of the following steps?

options.A: Uncoating of the virus in the endosome
options.B: Release of new virions from the infected cell

whyNot.A: **Amantadine**: acts here but only on influenza A with frequent resistance
whyNot.C: **Hemagglutinin**: viral attachment step, not the target of the usual oral drug
whyNot.D: **RNA polymerase / cap endonuclease**: a different target from the usual oral first-line drug
whyNot.E: **Nucleocapsid assembly**: not blocked by an approved drug in this setting

why: **Influenza treated with an oral neuraminidase inhibitor** (oseltamivir). It **blocks cleavage of sialic acid** on the host cell, so **new virions cannot be released** and spread.

drug.name: Oseltamivir
drug.how: Blocks viral neuraminidase, preventing release of progeny virions
drug.use: Influenza A and B (treatment and prophylaxis)
drug.watch: Nausea, vomiting; best within 48 hours of onset

stem: Researchers add a new antiviral to cultured human T cells infected with HIV-1. Electron microscopy of the budding virions shows immature particles with a ring-shaped core instead of the dense conical capsid. Viral RNA and proviral DNA levels are unchanged, and the particles are not infectious.
oneliner: Experiment: HIV-infected T cells + new drug + virions bud with immature ring-shaped cores, noninfectious + normal RNA and proviral DNA → what is blocked?
ask: The drug most likely inhibits which of the following processes?

options.A: Reverse transcription of viral RNA
options.B: Integration of viral DNA into host DNA
options.C: Cleavage of Gag-Pol polyprotein into functional proteins
options.D: Fusion of virus with the host cell membrane

whyNot.A: **RT inhibitors**: would lower proviral DNA, which is unchanged
whyNot.B: **Integrase inhibitors**: would lower integrated provirus, but virions would form normally
whyNot.D: **Enfuvirtide**: blocks entry, so no infected cells would be producing virions
whyNot.E: **Maraviroc**: entry step, before any viral production

answer: Gag-Pol cleavage by viral protease (protease inhibitor)
why: **Immature, noninfectious virions with normal viral nucleic acids** show a late block: **viral protease cannot cleave Gag-Pol**, so the mature core never forms (**protease inhibitor**).

drug.name: HIV protease inhibitors (-navirs)
drug.how: Block cleavage of the Gag-Pol polyprotein, producing immature noninfectious virions
drug.use: HIV, in combination therapy
drug.watch: Lipodystrophy, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, CYP3A4 inhibition (ritonavir)

stem: A pharmaceutical group screens a new compound that inhibits purified RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity in vitro. It has no effect on human DNA polymerases, viral neuraminidase, or herpesvirus thymidine kinase. The compound will be developed as an antiviral.
oneliner: Screening: new compound inhibits RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, spares human polymerases, neuraminidase and herpes TK → which virus would it treat?
ask: The compound would be most useful against infection with which of the following viruses?

options.A: HIV-1

whyNot.B: **HSV**: replicates with a viral DNA-dependent DNA polymerase; acyclovir covers it
whyNot.C: **Influenza**: an RNA virus using RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and neuraminidase
whyNot.D: **Adenovirus**: a DNA virus with DNA-dependent DNA polymerase
whyNot.E: **Poliovirus**: RNA virus using RNA-dependent RNA polymerase

why: **RNA-dependent DNA polymerase = reverse transcriptase**, the enzyme of **retroviruses such as HIV**. Other listed viruses use DNA- or RNA-dependent polymerases.

drug.name: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs, NNRTIs)
drug.how: Block RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, preventing viral DNA synthesis
drug.use: HIV, hepatitis B (NRTIs)
drug.watch: Class effects: NRTI marrow, lactic acidosis; NNRTI rash and CNS effects

stem: A 38-year-old man from southern China has had 3 months of vague right upper quadrant pain and mild jaundice. He often eats raw freshwater fish. Stool contains small operculated eggs and eosinophilia is present. A single-day oral drug is given that is also active against intestinal tapeworms.
oneliner: 38M + southern China + raw freshwater fish + RUQ pain, jaundice + operculated eggs + single-day drug that also covers tapeworms → how does it work?
ask: The drug most likely works by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding β-tubulin to block microtubule assembly
options.C: Depolarizing nicotinic receptors on the parasite
options.D: Increasing tegument permeability to calcium, causing paralysis

whyNot.A: **Albendazole**: mainly nematodes and cysts, less used for liver flukes
whyNot.B: **Ivermectin**: nematodes and ectoparasites, not flukes
whyNot.C: **Pyrantel pamoate**: nematodes only
whyNot.E: **Niclosamide**: intestinal tapeworms only, not tissue flukes

answer: Raises tegument calcium permeability, causing paralysis (praziquantel)
why: **Operculated eggs from raw freshwater fish** = Clonorchis, a liver fluke. **Praziquantel** treats flukes and tapeworms by **increasing calcium influx**, causing **spastic paralysis** of the parasite.

drug.name: Praziquantel
drug.how: Increases tegument calcium permeability, causing spastic paralysis
drug.use: Schistosomiasis, liver flukes, cysticercosis, tapeworms
drug.watch: Dizziness, headache, GI upset

stem: A 35-year-old man with HIV is switched to a once-daily pill containing efavirenz, emtricitabine and tenofovir. Two weeks later he reports vivid dreams and dizziness at bedtime. His pharmacist explains that all three drugs act on the same viral enzyme, but efavirenz, unlike the other two, works without being phosphorylated inside cells.
oneliner: 35M + HIV on efavirenz/emtricitabine/tenofovir + vivid dreams + all three hit one enzyme, efavirenz needs no phosphorylation → mechanism?
ask: Efavirenz acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Blocking integrase strand transfer

whyNot.A: **Integrase inhibitors** (dolutegravir): integrase is not the enzyme his two nucleoside analogs act on
whyNot.B: **Protease inhibitors** (darunavir): protease is not the enzyme his two nucleoside analogs act on
whyNot.D: **Enfuvirtide**: injected and binds gp41, a viral envelope protein, not an enzyme; efavirenz is an oral pill
whyNot.E: **Emtricitabine and tenofovir** act this way and **need phosphorylation**; efavirenz does not

why: All three drugs hit **reverse transcriptase**, but only efavirenz is **active without phosphorylation**, so it is a **non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor**. It binds an **allosteric pocket** beside the active site and does not compete with nucleotides. **Vivid dreams** and CNS effects are typical.

idea.rule: NNRTIs bind reverse transcriptase beside the active site, so they need no phosphorylation and do not compete with nucleotides.
also: Nevirapine, rilpivirine and doravirine are also NNRTIs
Nucleoside analogs (zidovudine, emtricitabine) need host kinases to activate them; tenofovir needs two phosphorylations
NNRTIs have no activity against HIV-2
Current first-line regimens are integrase inhibitor-based (e.g. bictegravir or dolutegravir plus two NRTIs)

drug.name: Efavirenz
drug.how: Binds reverse transcriptase at an allosteric site; no phosphorylation needed
drug.use: HIV-1 as part of a combination regimen
drug.watch: Vivid dreams, dizziness, depression, rash; CYP450 induction

stem: A 40-year-old man with HIV has detectable virus despite several regimens, and resistance testing shows multiple mutations. His physician adds a drug that he injects under the skin twice a day. He soon notices firm tender nodules at his injection sites.
oneliner: 40M + HIV with multidrug resistance + twice-daily subcutaneous injection + injection-site nodules → drug binds what?
ask: The added drug acts by binding which of the following?

options.A: Viral envelope gp41

whyNot.B: **Maraviroc**: oral, blocks the host CCR5 coreceptor; enfuvirtide is an injection that binds a viral protein
whyNot.C: **NRTIs and NNRTIs**: oral pills; they act on reverse transcriptase after entry
whyNot.D: **Protease inhibitors**: oral pills that act late, on new virions
whyNot.E: **Integrase inhibitors**: act after reverse transcription; none is a twice-daily subcutaneous injection

why: A **twice-daily subcutaneous** antiretroviral with **injection-site reactions** is **enfuvirtide**. It binds **gp41**, so the HIV envelope cannot fuse with the host cell membrane. It is kept for **salvage therapy**.

idea.rule: Entry inhibitors act before the virus gets inside: one blocks a viral protein, one a host protein.
also: Enfuvirtide binds viral gp41 (fusion)
Maraviroc blocks host CCR5 (needs CCR5-tropic virus)
gp120 binds CD4 and then the coreceptor
Integrase inhibitors act only after entry and reverse transcription

drug.name: Enfuvirtide
drug.how: Binds gp41 and stops fusion of the HIV envelope with the cell membrane
drug.use: Salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant HIV
drug.watch: Injection-site reactions (nodules, pain), hypersensitivity

stem: A 32-year-old woman with HIV needs a new drug added after treatment failure. A tropism assay on her blood shows that her virus enters cells only through CCR5. Her doctor chooses an oral entry inhibitor that acts on a protein of her own cells, not on a viral protein.
oneliner: 32F + HIV + tropism assay shows CCR5-tropic virus + oral entry inhibitor aimed at a host protein → target?
ask: The chosen drug acts by blocking which of the following?

options.A: Host CD4 receptor

whyNot.A: **CD4**: every HIV strain uses it, so tropism testing would not matter; the CD4-binding drug ibalizumab is an IV antibody, not oral
whyNot.B: **CXCR4**: used by X4-tropic virus; the assay here shows the virus uses **CCR5 only**
whyNot.C: **gp41**: a viral protein (enfuvirtide); the stem says the target is a **host** protein
whyNot.E: **gp120**: a viral protein; the stem says the target is a **host** protein

why: The drug needs a **tropism assay**, is an **entry inhibitor**, and hits a **host protein**: **maraviroc**, which blocks the **CCR5 coreceptor**. It works only against **CCR5-tropic** virus, not CXCR4 or dual-tropic virus.

idea.rule: A drug aimed at a host protein is only useful when the virus depends on that protein, so test first.
also: Maraviroc: check tropism before use
CCR5 delta-32 homozygotes resist HIV infection
Early infection uses CCR5; late infection can switch to CXCR4
Enfuvirtide acts on viral gp41, so no tropism test is needed

drug.name: Maraviroc
drug.how: Blocks the host CCR5 coreceptor so gp120 cannot complete entry
drug.use: CCR5-tropic HIV-1 after treatment failure
drug.watch: Tropism assay needed first; hepatotoxicity, orthostatic hypotension

stem: A 45-year-old man has had thick, yellow, crumbling toenails for over a year. A nail clipping stained with potassium hydroxide shows hyphae. Because he takes simvastatin, his doctor avoids drugs that strongly inhibit CYP3A4 and prescribes an oral antifungal for 12 weeks, orders baseline liver tests, and warns that it may change his sense of taste.
oneliner: 45M + thick yellow crumbling toenails + KOH hyphae + 12-wk oral antifungal, no CYP3A4 inhibition, LFTs, taste change → target?
ask: The prescribed drug inhibits which of the following fungal targets?

options.A: Lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase
options.E: Microtubule assembly in the mitotic spindle

whyNot.A: **Azoles** (itraconazole) also treat nails, but they **strongly inhibit CYP3A4**, which the doctor avoided
whyNot.C: **Echinocandins** (caspofungin): IV only, for Candida and Aspergillus; this drug is oral
whyNot.D: **Flucytosine**: becomes 5-FU; used with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis, not nails
whyNot.E: **Griseofulvin**: needs many months to a year or more for toenails, not a 12-week course

why: A **12-week oral course for dermatophyte onychomycosis** with **liver tests, taste change** and no CYP3A4 inhibition is **terbinafine**. It inhibits **squalene epoxidase**, so **squalene accumulates** (toxic to the fungus) and **ergosterol falls**.

idea.rule: Antifungals that hit ergosterol synthesis act at different enzymes along one pathway.
also: Terbinafine: squalene epoxidase
Azoles: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase
Polyenes bind ergosterol itself
Echinocandins hit the cell wall (glucan synthase), not ergosterol

drug.name: Terbinafine
drug.how: Inhibits squalene epoxidase, so squalene builds up and ergosterol falls
drug.use: Onychomycosis and other dermatophyte infections
drug.watch: Hepatotoxicity, taste disturbance

stem: A 35-year-old man with AIDS has headache, fever and neck stiffness. India ink of the cerebrospinal fluid shows encapsulated yeasts. He is given IV amphotericin B for induction together with a second drug that his own cells cannot activate; only the fungus converts it to its active form. His blood counts are monitored closely.
oneliner: 35M + AIDS + cryptococcal meningitis + amphotericin B plus a second drug activated by a fungal enzyme + blood counts monitored → process blocked?
ask: The second drug acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Binding ergosterol to form membrane pores
options.D: Binding tubulin in the mitotic spindle
options.E: Inhibiting fungal DNA and RNA synthesis

whyNot.A: **Amphotericin B** itself forms pores; this is the first drug, not the second
whyNot.B: **Terbinafine**: needs no fungal activation, and is used for dermatophytes, not meningitis
whyNot.C: **Caspofungin**: needs no fungal activation, does not reach the CSF and has no activity against Cryptococcus
whyNot.D: **Griseofulvin**: dermatophyte drug that needs no fungal activation

why: **Cryptococcal meningitis induction = amphotericin B + flucytosine**. Fungal **cytosine deaminase** converts flucytosine to **5-fluorouracil**, which blocks **thymidylate synthase** and corrupts RNA. Human cells lack the enzyme, but **bone marrow suppression** still occurs.

idea.rule: A prodrug activated only by a pathogen enzyme is selective, but not harmless.
also: Flucytosine: fungal cytosine deaminase makes 5-FU
Acyclovir: viral thymidine kinase activates it
Metronidazole: reduced only in anaerobes
Isoniazid: activated by mycobacterial KatG

drug.name: Flucytosine
drug.how: Fungal cytosine deaminase converts it to 5-FU, which inhibits thymidylate synthase and fungal DNA/RNA synthesis
drug.use: Cryptococcal meningitis with amphotericin B
drug.watch: Bone marrow suppression, GI upset

stem: An 8-year-old boy has scaly, patchy hair loss on his scalp with broken hairs. Hairs fluoresce under Wood lamp and show spores on microscopy. His doctor prescribes an oral drug for several months, which deposits in keratin-containing tissue and can lower the effect of his other medications.
oneliner: 8M + scaly patchy scalp hair loss, broken hairs + fungal spores on hair + months-long oral drug that deposits in keratin → mechanism?
ask: The prescribed drug stops fungal growth by which of the following?

options.A: Binding tubulin to block the mitotic spindle
options.B: Binding ergosterol to form membrane pores
options.D: Blocking squalene epoxidase to deplete ergosterol
options.E: Inhibiting beta-1,3-glucan synthase in the cell wall

whyNot.B: **Amphotericin B or nystatin**: not absorbed orally and not used for hair infection
whyNot.C: **Azoles**: inhibit P450 and raise other drug levels; this drug lowers their effect
whyNot.D: **Terbinafine**: also treats tinea capitis, but it does not induce P450 or lower other drugs' effects
whyNot.E: **Caspofungin**: IV echinocandin for invasive Candida and Aspergillus

answer: Binding tubulin to disrupt the mitotic spindle (griseofulvin)
why: **Tinea capitis** treated for months with a drug that **deposits in keratin** and **induces cytochrome P450** is **griseofulvin**. It **binds microtubules**, disrupting the **mitotic spindle** of dermatophytes.

idea.rule: Griseofulvin is the antifungal that acts on microtubules and concentrates in keratin.
also: Induces P450, lowering warfarin and oral contraceptive levels
Teratogenic and carcinogenic concerns
Reserved for dermatophytes of skin, hair, nails
Can cause headaches and disulfiram-like reaction

drug.name: Griseofulvin
drug.how: Binds tubulin and disrupts the mitotic spindle; deposits in keratin
drug.use: Tinea capitis and other dermatophyte infections
drug.watch: CYP450 induction, teratogenicity, headache, hepatotoxicity

stem: An 82-year-old woman living in a nursing home has abrupt fever, cough and myalgias during an outbreak, and rapid testing shows influenza A. Her physician explains that an older oral antiviral, which acts early in the viral life cycle and works only on influenza A, is no longer recommended because nearly all circulating strains resist it.
oneliner: 82F + nursing home influenza A + older oral drug, early-acting, influenza A only, no longer used due to resistance → step blocked?
ask: The older drug blocks which of the following steps?

options.A: Uncoating after endosomal entry
options.E: Protease cleavage of a viral polyprotein

whyNot.B: **Acyclovir and ganciclovir** target viral DNA polymerase; influenza has an RNA genome
whyNot.C: **Oseltamivir and zanamivir** block neuraminidase release of new virions; this drug acts earlier
whyNot.D: **Reverse transcription**: a retroviral step, not in influenza
whyNot.E: **Protease cleavage**: HIV and hepatitis C; not influenza

answer: Uncoating (M2 ion channel blocked by amantadine)
why: **Influenza A only + early-acting + near-universal resistance** = **amantadine** (or rimantadine). It blocks the **M2 proton channel**, so the virus cannot acidify its core in the endosome and **uncoat**. It is **no longer recommended** for influenza; neuraminidase inhibitors are used instead.

idea.rule: Each anti-influenza drug blocks one step of the viral cycle.
also: Amantadine, rimantadine: M2 channel, uncoating, influenza A only
Oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir: neuraminidase, release of new virions
Baloxavir: cap-dependent endonuclease, viral mRNA synthesis
Adamantane resistance comes from an M2 mutation (S31N)

drug.name: Amantadine
drug.how: Blocks the influenza A M2 proton channel, preventing uncoating
drug.use: Parkinson disease; no longer recommended for influenza because of resistance
drug.watch: Ataxia, livedo reticularis, CNS effects, anticholinergic effects

stem: A 24-year-old woman has itchy, frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge and a red, speckled cervix. Vaginal pH is 6.2 and a wet mount shows motile flagellated organisms. She receives a single oral dose of a drug that is inactive against aerobic bacteria and is told to avoid alcohol for the next 48 hours.
oneliner: 24F + frothy green discharge + pH 6.2 + motile flagellates + drug inactive against aerobes, alcohol warning → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains how this drug kills the organism?

options.A: Binds the 30S ribosomal subunit and blocks aminoacyl-tRNA entry
options.B: Inhibits DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and prevents supercoiling
options.C: Reduced to toxic free radicals that fragment the organism's DNA
options.D: Blocks dihydropteroate synthase and folate synthesis
options.E: Binds the 50S ribosomal subunit and blocks translocation

whyNot.A: Mechanism of **tetracyclines**; they are not the single-dose treatment for **trichomoniasis**
whyNot.B: Mechanism of **fluoroquinolones**, which cover aerobes; the drug here is **inactive against aerobic bacteria**
whyNot.D: Mechanism of **sulfonamides**, which act on aerobic bacteria and do not need **anaerobic reduction**
whyNot.E: Mechanism of **macrolides and clindamycin**, which act on aerobic gram-positive bacteria; the drug here is **inactive against aerobes**

answer: Reduction to toxic free radicals that damage DNA
why: The drug is a **prodrug activated only under low-redox (anaerobic) conditions**, so it is active against **anaerobes and protozoa** such as *Trichomonas*. Its reduced radical metabolites **fragment DNA**, and it blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, hence the **alcohol warning**.

drug.name: Metronidazole
drug.how: Reduced in anaerobes and protozoa to free radicals that damage DNA
drug.use: Trichomoniasis, bacterial vaginosis, giardiasis, amebiasis, C. difficile, anaerobic infections below the diaphragm
drug.watch: Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, metallic taste, peripheral neuropathy, headache

idea.rule: Antimicrobial mechanisms match the organism's metabolism: anaerobic activation limits a drug to anaerobes and protozoa.
also: Aminoglycosides need oxygen-dependent uptake, so they fail against anaerobes
Clindamycin covers anaerobes above the diaphragm by 50S blockade, not DNA damage
Tinidazole: same class and mechanism as metronidazole

stem: A 37-year-old nurse is started on a three-drug regimen after a needlestick from a patient with HIV. Three weeks later she is fatigued and pale. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL and the neutrophil count is 900/mm3. Two of her drugs must be phosphorylated by host cell kinases before they become active.
oneliner: 37F nurse + HIV needlestick on 3-drug prophylaxis + anemia + neutropenia + drugs needing host kinase activation → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains the antiviral action of the drug most likely responsible for her blood counts?

options.A: Blocks strand transfer of proviral DNA into the host genome
options.B: Lacks a 3'-OH group, terminating the growing proviral DNA chain
options.C: Prevents cleavage of the gag-pol polyprotein into functional proteins
options.D: Prevents gp41-mediated fusion of viral and host cell membranes
options.E: Blocks the CCR5 coreceptor used for viral entry into CD4 cells

whyNot.A: **Integrase inhibitors** (raltegravir) are well tolerated and do not need **kinase phosphorylation** or cause marrow suppression
whyNot.C: **Protease inhibitors** cause **metabolic effects and drug interactions**, not marrow suppression, and need no phosphorylation
whyNot.D: **Enfuvirtide** is injected and acts on **gp41**; it is not a prodrug phosphorylated by kinases
whyNot.E: **Maraviroc** acts on the host **CCR5** receptor and is not phosphorylated or marrow-toxic

answer: Chain termination of proviral DNA (no 3'-OH group)
why: The drug is a **nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor** (zidovudine). After **phosphorylation by host kinases** it is incorporated into proviral DNA but has **no 3'-OH**, so the chain cannot extend. Zidovudine also inhibits marrow precursors, causing **anemia and neutropenia**.

drug.name: Zidovudine (AZT)
drug.how: Phosphorylated to a triphosphate lacking a 3'-OH, causing proviral DNA chain termination
drug.use: HIV treatment, needlestick prophylaxis and prevention of mother-to-child transmission
drug.watch: Bone marrow suppression (anemia, neutropenia), myopathy, lactic acidosis

idea.rule: NRTIs and the nucleotide analog tenofovir all act as chain terminators of proviral DNA.
also: Tenofovir is the only nucleotide (already monophosphorylated) analog
Lamivudine and emtricitabine also terminate the chain
NRTIs are also used in hepatitis B (lamivudine, tenofovir)
